42867539.label: Purpose
42867539.text: Accurate intraoperative assessment of radiofrequency ablation (RFA) margins in hepatic malignancies remains a significant clinical challenge.

42867539.label: Methods
42867539.text: This study investigates the efficacy of hyperspectral imaging (HSI) for objective, spatially resolved discrimination of ablated tissue, viable tumor, and normal parenchyma in 10 ex vivo liver specimens. Analysis of visible-near-infrared (VNIR) reflectance revealed distinct spectral signatures, characterized by a consistent monotonic hierarchy (ablated < normal < tumor), enabling reliable tissue differentiation. Segmentation performance was systematically evaluated using four supervised classifiers: Spectral Angle Mapper (SAM), Support Vector Machine (SVM), Random Forest (RF), and Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA). The total delineated tissue area exhibited notable inter-method variability, ranging from 137,283 to 189,289 pixels (+ 37.9%), underscoring sensitivity to classifier architecture.

42867539.label: Results
42867539.text: Nevertheless, all approaches maintained biologically coherent tissue distributions, with normal parenchyma predominating (44-56%), followed by tumor (25-39%) and ablated regions (17-20%). That is consistently indicating the necessity for monitoring ablative margins. SAM, SVM, and LDA classifiers achieved class-specific detection errors around 3.5% and 18%. LDA attained the highest overall accuracy (94.5%), demonstrating the potential of HSI for reliable, intraoperative image-guided tissue characterization. Dimensionality reduction across 462 spectral bands identified an optimal discriminative window within 643-698 nm, supporting the development of streamlined multispectral systems.

42867539.label: Conclusion
42867539.text: Overall, HSI is neither a contact nor destructive modality for quantitative RFA assessment. Despite classifier-dependent variability necessitating standardized or ensemble strategies, these findings support its prospective integration into real-time surgical guidance, pending in vivo validation.

42965589.label: Purpose
42965589.text: To develop an additive ctSLEP score from routine CT morphologic invasion signs and evaluate the complementary value of morphologic CT, quantitative spectral CT, and systemic inflammation for pretreatment prediction of neoadjuvant therapy (NAT) response in locally advanced gastric cancer (LAGC).

42965589.label: Methods
42965589.text: This retrospective study included 158 patients with LAGC who underwent NAT and radical gastrectomy and were randomly divided into training and internal validation cohorts (7:3). Becker tumor regression grade 1a/1b defined response and 2/3 nonresponse. Additive ctSLEP summed four pretreatment CT signs: serosal invasion, extramural venous invasion, subtle signs of occult peritoneal/omental involvement, and lymphovascular invasion. Five hierarchical models combined additive ctSLEP, venous-phase iodine concentration (ICVP), arterial enhancement fraction (AEF), and neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR). Performance was assessed using AUC, Brier score, calibration, and prespecified paired DeLong comparisons. A chemotherapy-only sensitivity analysis was performed.

42965589.label: Results
42965589.text: Sixty-five patients (41.1%) were responders and ninety-three (58.9%) nonresponders. In the internal validation cohort, AUCs for the Morphology, Spectral, Imaging, Clinical-spectral, and Combined models were 0.642, 0.741, 0.725, 0.713, and 0.754, respectively. The Combined model had the highest AUC and lowest Brier score (0.200). Adding spectral CT to morphology increased AUC by 0.083 (P=0.129), and adding additive ctSLEP to the Clinical-spectral model increased AUC by 0.041 (P=0.558). In 51 patients receiving chemotherapy alone, higher additive ctSLEP was associated with greater odds of nonresponse (OR=2.15, 95% CI 1.35-3.88), whereas higher ICVP was associated with lower odds (OR=0.83, 95% CI 0.69-0.96).

42965589.label: Conclusion
42965589.text: The combined model showed reasonable predictive performance in internal validation. These findings support further external evaluation of a low-dimensional, clinically interpretable strategy integrating morphologic invasion burden, spectral enhancement, and systemic inflammation for pretreatment NAT response stratification.

42975389.text: The Excessive Radiation Dose or Inadequate Image Quality for Diagnostic CT in Adults (ExRad) measure is the first automated radiology outcome measure adopted by CMS. We describe its development, specification, calculation, and adoption. Beginning in 2018, the measure was developed under a CMS cooperative agreement following the Measures Management System Blueprint, with oversight from a multidisciplinary Technical Expert Panel. ExRad evaluates each adult diagnostic CT examination in three steps. First, the examination is assigned to 1 of 19 CT categories defined by anatomic region and clinical indication using International Classification of Diseases, 10th Revision, Clinical Modification and Current Procedural Terminology codes. Second, size-adjusted radiation dose and image noise are computed from the DICOM dose report and pixel data; because clinical and radiology data reside in separate systems, translation software inside the hospital firewall performs the linkage and calculations automatically. Third, dose and noise are compared with category-specific thresholds derived from a reader study in which 125 radiologists rated the image quality of 734 CT examinations. An examination is out of range if either value exceeds its threshold, and the measure score is the percentage of eligible examinations that are out of range. Testing across 32 facilities in eight health systems confirmed the availability, accuracy, validity, and reproducibility of all data elements, and the National Quality Forum endorsed the measure in 2021. CMS adopted ExRad in 2023 into hospital inpatient, hospital outpatient, and clinician quality reporting programs, with voluntary reporting beginning in 2025. It is the sole outcome measure in the Diagnostic Radiology MIPS (Merit-Based Incentive Payment System) Value Pathway.

42983139.label: Objectives
42983139.text: To develop and externally validate a predictive model integrating multiphasic CT radiomics and clinical variables to estimate recurrence risk after first-episode acute pancreatitis (AP).

42983139.label: Materials and methods
42983139.text: This multicenter retrospective study included 548 patients with first-episode AP (training, n = 272; internal validation, n = 117; external validation, n = 159). Clinical and multiphasic CT data were collected, with recurrence as the primary endpoint. After stability-based feature selection, clinical, radiomics, and combined Cox models were constructed. Performance was evaluated using the C-index and time-dependent AUC, with SHAP for interpretability.

42983139.label: Results
42983139.text: A total of 548 patients were included (median age 42 years; 363 men). Recurrence rates were similar across cohorts (30.1%, 29.9%, and 28.3%; p = 0.702). The combined model achieved C-indices of 0.783 and 0.775 in the internal and external validation cohorts, respectively, numerically higher than those of the clinical model (0.748 and 0.750) and radiomics model (0.647 and 0.619), although the incremental improvement over the clinical model was not statistically significant. In the external validation cohort, time-dependent AUCs remained acceptable through 36 months but declined at 48 months. High-risk patients had lower 3-year recurrence-free survival than low-risk patients (37.4% vs 86.8%; log-rank p < 0.001). SHAP analysis identified the NC-3mm-Radscore as the most influential imaging-derived variable, whereas etiology-targeted prevention was the dominant protective factor.

42983139.label: Conclusions
42983139.text: The combined model demonstrated acceptable discrimination for predicting recurrence within the first 24 months after first-episode AP and may facilitate individualized follow-up and secondary prevention strategies.

42983139.label: Key points
42983139.text: Question Can a multiphasic CT radiomics-clinical model improve prediction of AP recurrence over clinical factors alone in a multicenter setting? Findings The combined model demonstrated numerically higher predictive performance than the clinical model, though the incremental improvement was not statistically significant. Critical relevance statement This study critically evaluates the added value of multiphasic radiomics for recurrence prediction in AP, demonstrating that while radiomics captures baseline microenvironmental vulnerability, post-discharge clinical interventions remain the dominant dynamic drivers.

43002589.text: A 54-year-old man with back pain showed lytic vertebral lesions on MRI. 18F-FDG PET/CT revealed an FDG-avid thyroid primary, skeletal metastases, and a relatively low FDG-avid right renal lesion. Thyroid histopathology confirmed follicular carcinoma. Post-thyroidectomy radioiodine scan demonstrated intense uptake in both skeletal and renal lesions. Biopsy from the renal lesion confirmed renal metastasis. Renal involvement in differentiated thyroid cancer is rare and may demonstrate concordant FDG and radioiodine avidity.

43034939.label: Objectives
43034939.text: To compare conventional and delayed (≥ 30 min) hepatobiliary-phase (HBP) gadoxetate-enhanced MRI for the detection of bile leaks.

43034939.label: Materials and methods
43034939.text: This retrospective single-center study included all consecutive gadoxetate-enhanced MRI examinations comprising delayed HBP acquisitions performed for suspected biliary leak over 2 years at a tertiary hepatobiliary referral center. Two abdominal radiologists blinded to clinical records independently assessed leak presence at each timepoint. A composite reference standard incorporating endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography, surgical exploration, percutaneous drainage findings, and multidisciplinary assessment was utilized to assign ground-truth leak status. Sensitivity, specificity, positive and negative predictive values (PPV, NPV), accuracy, and inter-reader agreement were calculated.

43034939.label: Results
43034939.text: Thirty-five patients (22 men; median age, 56 years; interquartile range (IQR), 48-65) undergoing 36 examinations were included. The most common indications were liver transplantation (n = 13/35, 37%) and cholecystectomy (n = 11/35, 31%). Conventional and delayed HBP were acquired at a median of 21 and 65 min after injection, respectively. Twenty-two of 36 examinations (61%) were ground-truth positive. Inter-reader agreement was perfect for conventional HBP (κ = 1.00) and excellent for delayed HBP (κ = 0.94; 95% CI 0.84-1.00). Conventional HBP demonstrated 27% sensitivity (95% CI 11-50%), 100% specificity (95% CI 77-100%), and 56% accuracy (95% CI 38-72%). Delayed HBP demonstrated 82% sensitivity (95% CI 60-95%), 100% specificity (95% CI 77-100%), and 89% accuracy (95% CI 74-97%). NPV increased from 47% to 78%. Delayed HBP yielded higher sensitivity and overall accuracy than conventional HBP (p < 0.001, exact McNemar tests).

43034939.label: Conclusion
43034939.text: Delayed HBP improved bile leak detection without loss of specificity.

43034939.label: Key points
43034939.text: Question Does extending gadoxetate hepatobiliary-phase MRI acquisitions beyond the conventional 20-min window improve the detection of active bile leaks? Findings Delayed hepatobiliary-phase imaging raised sensitivity for bile leak detection from 27% to 82% without loss of specificity, highlighting acquisition timing as a key diagnostic determinant. Clinical relevance Delayed gadoxetate hepatobiliary-phase imaging is an effective adjunct for detecting active bile leaks and should be considered when findings at conventional timing are negative or equivocal, with direct implications for clinical management.

43037689.label: Purpose
43037689.text: To determine which MRI features used in the diagnosis of adenomyosis are reproducible between readers, and whether a diagnostic certainty scale used in routine reporting can be applied consistently.

43037689.label: Methods
43037689.text: Prospective single-center study of 108 consecutive women referred for 3-T pelvic MRI after transvaginal ultrasound suspicion of adenomyosis. Three subspecialized radiologists, with 10, 8 and 5 years of experience, independently assessed all examinations, blinded to clinical data, ultrasound findings and to each other. Diagnostic certainty was recorded on a four-level ordinal scale (definite, probable, possible, absent). Agreement was quantified with Fleiss' kappa for the three readers, Cohen's kappa for pairs, and weighted kappa for ordinal variables.

43037689.label: Results
43037689.text: Agreement for the four-level scale was fair when unweighted (κ = 0.401) and substantial when quadratic-weighted (mean 0.663). No patient was rated probable by all three readers, and agreement across the definite-versus-probable boundary was null (κ = -0.013 to 0.143); collapsing the two categories raised it to κ = 0.581-0.698. For the two direct criteria it was substantial for myometrial hemorrhagic foci (κ = 0.650) and moderate for myometrial cysts (κ = 0.555). Among junctional zone measurements, agreement was moderate for thickness > 12 mm (κ = 0.530) but absent for junctional zone irregularity (κ = 0.048), which was non-evaluable in 21 of 108 examinations (19.4%). These examinations showed a higher prevalence of motion artifacts (p = 0.0005). Agreement on severity grade was moderate (κ = 0.441).

43037689.label: Conclusion
43037689.text: Reproducibility varied widely across MRI features of adenomyosis, and the intermediate levels of the diagnostic certainty scale were not applied consistently. These findings argue for redefining the current MRI criteria for adenomyosis.

43040039.label: Purpose
43040039.text: To evaluate the prevalence of pre-procedural US-MRI discordance and its association with Society of Interventional Radiology (SIR)-standardized outcomes in patients undergoing US-guided high-intensity focused ultrasound (HIFU) ablation for symptomatic uterine fibroids.

43040039.label: Materials and methods
43040039.text: 308 consecutive patients were included. Discordance was defined as mismatch in fibroid type, location, uterine position, or absolute volume percentage difference > 50%. Patients were stratified into concordant (n = 252) and discordant (n = 56) groups. Outcomes were assessed according to SIR domains: technical success (non-perfused volume ratio on day-1 contrast-enhanced MRI), technical efficacy (through six procedural surrogates as a whole: energy-efficiency factor, overall treatment time, cumulative sonication time, treatment intensity, average sonication power, and oxytocin dose), adverse events (SIR classification), and favorable short-term procedural outcome.

43040039.label: Results
43040039.text: Discordance occurred in 18.2% of cases. Categorical agreement was high, with Gwet's AC1 > 0.93, and volume agreement was good, with an intraclass correlation coefficient of 0.773. Day-1 non-perfused volume ratio and technical-success thresholds were comparable between groups. In unadjusted analysis, the energy-efficiency factor was higher after discordant imaging (p = 0.024) and oxytocin use was shifted toward the 60 IU dose (p = 0.036). After adjustment, neither association remained significant (p = 0.191 and 0.228). Adverse-event profiles and the favorable short-term procedural outcome did not differ significantly.

43040039.label: Conclusion
43040039.text: In this study, pre-HIFU US-MRI discordance was not associated with clear differences in technical success, technical efficacy, adverse events, or short-term procedural outcomes. Recognition of discordance may still help inform procedural planning and patient counseling within SIR-standardized frameworks.
